claim: Co-morbidity and co-occurrence of disease traits are often determined by shared genetic and molecular mechanisms.
source: There is growing recognition that co-morbidity and co-occurrence of disease traits are often determined by shared genetic and molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established recognition in the field.

claim: Genetic variation in the Klf7 gene may influence gene transcripts in bone marrow-derived myeloid cells.
source: our method predicts that genetic variation in the Klf7 gene may influence gene transcripts in bone marrow-derived myeloid cells, which in turn affect 17 behavioral traits following morphine injection
evidence: This prediction is stated in the abstract as a result of the GEMOT method.

claim: Klf7-influenced transcripts in bone marrow-derived myeloid cells affect 17 behavioral traits following morphine injection.
source: our method predicts that genetic variation in the Klf7 gene may influence gene transcripts in bone marrow-derived myeloid cells, which in turn affect 17 behavioral traits following morphine injection
evidence: This is a prediction from the GEMOT analysis stated in the abstract.

claim: The predicted effect of Klf7 is consistent with in vitro perturbation of Klf7 in bone marrow cells.
source: this predicted effect of Klf7 is consistent with an in vitro perturbation of Klf7 in bone marrow cells
evidence: The abstract states that experimental perturbation data supports the prediction.

claim: Connections among diseases are typically attributable to a common underlying genetic or molecular mechanism.
source: Various studies have shown that such connections among diseases are typically attributable to a common underlying genetic or molecular mechanism (Rzhetsky et al., 2007; Oti et al., 2008; Barabási et al., 2011; Cotsapas et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Understanding common mechanisms among disease phenotypes allows for improved disease classification and treatment.
source: Disclosure of unexpected relationships among disease phenotypes and understanding of their common mechanisms opens the way to improved disease classification and treatment.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of understanding disease mechanisms.

claim: Understanding common mechanisms may allow a drug approved for one disease to be used for the treatment of another disease.
source: In particular, it may allow a drug approved for one disease to be used for the treatment of another disease, and provide us with the means to anticipate undesired off-target effects (e.g., Ashburn and Thor, 2004; Dudley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on drug repurposing.

claim: Understanding common mechanisms provides means to anticipate undesired off-target effects.
source: In particular, it may allow a drug approved for one disease to be used for the treatment of another disease, and provide us with the means to anticipate undesired off-target effects (e.g., Ashburn and Thor, 2004; Dudley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of understanding disease mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Relying entirely on trait information makes it difficult to identify shared mechanisms and distinguish shared molecular mechanisms from shared environmental influences.
source: Relying entirely on trait information, however, makes it difficult to identify the shared mechanisms and to distinguish shared molecular mechanisms from shared environmental influences.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of trait-based approaches.

claim: Gene-based approaches that use pairwise gene-trait connections have two major drawbacks.
source: Notably, although such 'gene-based' approaches provide a list of putative non-environmental mechanisms, their utilization has two major drawbacks.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of existing gene-based methods.

claim: Gene-based approaches assign a single mechanistic layer whereas genetic variation affects multiple molecular components.
source: First, these approaches assign a single mechanistic layer whereas in fact what is affected by genetic variation is a number of molecular components (such as transcripts), which affect the physiological traits secondarily; thus, the model should include a series of mechanistic layers and the propagation of information between them.
evidence: This is stated as the first drawback of gene-based approaches.

claim: Gene-based approaches do not distinguish between reactive, independent, and causative relationships.
source: Secondly, gene-based approaches do not distinguish between reactive, independent, and causative relationships, whereas molecular components should be related causatively to the group of traits.
evidence: This is stated as the second drawback of gene-based approaches.

claim: GEMOT constructs three-layer modules consisting of a group of molecular mechanisms translating between a genetic layer and a layer of traits.
source: GEMOT addresses the above challenges by constructing three-layer modules in which each module consists of a group of molecular mechanisms (here, gene transcripts within a 'transcripts layer') translating between a genetic layer and a layer of traits.
evidence: This describes the structure of GEMOT modules.

claim: A GEMOT module includes only transcripts that are part of causative relationships (driver transcripts).
source: In particular, a GEMOT module is focused specifically on causative, non-environmental relationships rather than on relationships of any kind, and accordingly it includes only transcripts that are part of causative relationships (referred to as 'driver transcripts', see Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes a key feature of GEMOT modules, with reference to figures.

claim: Detailed reconstruction of all relationships among variants, traits and transcripts is a major computational and statistical burden.
source: However, such a detailed reconstruction is a major computational and statistical burden, especially considering the large number of components.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge that GEMOT addresses.

claim: GEMOT uses a stepwise heuristic approach that reduces the search space and allows scalability to large networks.
source: This problem is avoided in GEMOT by the use of a stepwise heuristic approach that drastically reduces the search space and allows scalability to large networks.
evidence: This describes how GEMOT addresses computational challenges.

claim: GEMOT was applied to 1738 traits spanning a broad spectrum of physiological, biochemical, clinical, and behavioral traits measured across genotyped BXD mouse recombinant inbred strains.
source: We applied GEMOT to a large dataset of 1738 traits spanning a broad spectrum of physiological, biochemical, clinical, and behavioral traits that were measured across the genotyped BXD mouse recombinant inbred strains (a cross between the C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains [Wang et al., 2003]).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study, with citation.

claim: BXD mouse recombinant inbred strains are a cross between the C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains.
source: We applied GEMOT to a large dataset of 1738 traits spanning a broad spectrum of physiological, biochemical, clinical, and behavioral traits that were measured across the genotyped BXD mouse recombinant inbred strains (a cross between the C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains [Wang et al., 2003]).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the BXD strains, with citation.

claim: Transcript levels were measured in bone marrow-derived myeloid cells.
source: We used measurements of transcript levels in bone marrow-derived myeloid cells (Gerrits et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the molecular data used, with citation.

claim: Many of the GEMOT findings were supported by independent knowledge or data.
source: Notably, many of the findings were supported by independent knowledge or data.
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the results.

claim: The tissue specificity of modules was demonstrated based on post-processing analysis of gene expression in additional tissues.
source: We also demonstrated the tissue specificity of modules, based on a post-processing analysis of gene expression in additional tissues.
evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed in the study.

claim: GEMOT consists of three main stages.
source: GEMOT consists of three main stages (see 'Materials and methods', Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the structure of the GEMOT algorithm.

claim: In stage I, GEMOT identifies bipartite modules consisting of a single genomic interval and multiple traits connected by linked relationships through certain transcripts.
source: In stage I, GEMOT identifies 'bipartite modules' consisting of a single genomic interval and multiple traits that are connected by linked relationships through certain transcripts (e.g., traits p1, p3, p4 and variant v1 in Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This describes the first stage of GEMOT with reference to a figure.

claim: In stage II, candidate transcripts are added to the modules based on their linked relationships.
source: In stage II, candidate transcripts are added to the modules solely on the basis of their linked relationships (e.g., candidate transcripts g1–g3, Figure 1A, middle); the resulting 'tripartite modules', however, are not limited to causative relationships.
evidence: This describes the second stage of GEMOT with reference to a figure.

claim: In stage III, GEMOT refines the tripartite modules by investigating causal relationships and eliminating non-causative transcripts.
source: Finally, in stage III, GEMOT refines the tripartite modules by investigating the causal relationships within them and eliminating non-causative transcripts.
evidence: This describes the third stage of GEMOT.

claim: The output GEMOT module consists of validated driver transcripts, the traits they affect, and a single causal genomic interval.
source: The output GEMOT module, therefore, finally consists of the validated driver transcripts, the trait(s) they affect, and a single causal genomic interval (e.g., driver transcripts g1, g3; traits p1, p4; variant v1 in Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This describes the final output of GEMOT with reference to a figure.

claim: GEMOT found 40 bipartite modules with permutation-based FDR < 10^-3.
source: Using GEMOT, we found 40 bipartite modules, 11 tripartite modules, and 8 mature GEMOT modules with non-overlapping sets of drivers (permutation-based FDR < 10−3, 'Materials and methods'; see Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: This reports the number of modules found with statistical significance.

claim: GEMOT found 11 tripartite modules with permutation-based FDR < 10^-3.
source: Using GEMOT, we found 40 bipartite modules, 11 tripartite modules, and 8 mature GEMOT modules with non-overlapping sets of drivers (permutation-based FDR < 10−3, 'Materials and methods'; see Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: This reports the number of modules found with statistical significance.

claim: GEMOT found 8 mature GEMOT modules with non-overlapping sets of drivers and permutation-based FDR < 10^-3.
source: Using GEMOT, we found 40 bipartite modules, 11 tripartite modules, and 8 mature GEMOT modules with non-overlapping sets of drivers (permutation-based FDR < 10−3, 'Materials and methods'; see Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: This reports the number of modules found with statistical significance.

claim: No GEMOT modules were found in 100 permutation tests.
source: For comparison, no GEMOT modules were found in 100 permutation tests, and the average number of bipartite and tripartite modules in 100 permutation tests was 32 and 0.06, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This provides negative control results from permutation testing.

claim: The average number of bipartite modules in 100 permutation tests was 32.
source: For comparison, no GEMOT modules were found in 100 permutation tests, and the average number of bipartite and tripartite modules in 100 permutation tests was 32 and 0.06, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This provides negative control results from permutation testing.

claim: The average number of tripartite modules in 100 permutation tests was 0.06.
source: For comparison, no GEMOT modules were found in 100 permutation tests, and the average number of bipartite and tripartite modules in 100 permutation tests was 32 and 0.06, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This provides negative control results from permutation testing.

claim: The observed link potential scores in mice were much higher than expected by chance (p < 10^-10).
source: As expected, the observed link potential scores in mice were much higher than would be expected by chance (p < 10−10, permutation test; Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This reports statistical significance of the link potential scores.

claim: It is highly unlikely that GEMOT modules were generated at random (p < 0.01).
source: It is highly unlikely, therefore, that our GEMOT modules were generated at random (p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical conclusion based on permutation testing.

claim: Modules nos. 1-3, 6-8 show strong correlations between traits.
source: Notably modules nos. 1–3, 6–8 show strong correlations between traits, whereas the remaining modules show moderate or weak trait–trait correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This characterizes the trait correlations in different modules with reference to a figure.

claim: The remaining modules (4, 5) show moderate or weak trait-trait correlations.
source: Notably modules nos. 1–3, 6–8 show strong correlations between traits, whereas the remaining modules show moderate or weak trait–trait correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This characterizes the trait correlations in different modules with reference to a figure.

claim: Five of the modules relate to morphine responses (nos. 2, 5-8).
source: Notably, the trait collections of the different modules are partly overlapping. For example, five of the modules relate to morphine responses (nos. 2, 5–8) and two modules relate to thermal nociception (nos. 3 and 5).
evidence: This describes the overlap in trait types across modules.

claim: Two modules relate to thermal nociception (nos. 3 and 5).
source: Notably, the trait collections of the different modules are partly overlapping. For example, five of the modules relate to morphine responses (nos. 2, 5–8) and two modules relate to thermal nociception (nos. 3 and 5).
evidence: This describes the overlap in trait types across modules.

claim: There is no overlap between the drivers and variants of the different modules.
source: Nevertheless, although some of the modules have overlapping traits, there is no overlap between the drivers and variants of the different modules (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1B), demonstrating GEMOT's ability to predict several distinct underlying mechanisms for the same collection of traits.
evidence: This describes a key finding about module distinctness with reference to figures.

claim: GEMOT can predict several distinct underlying mechanisms for the same collection of traits.
source: Nevertheless, although some of the modules have overlapping traits, there is no overlap between the drivers and variants of the different modules (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1B), demonstrating GEMOT's ability to predict several distinct underlying mechanisms for the same collection of traits.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of GEMOT demonstrated by the results.

claim: Module no. 2 consists of 17 different traits measured following treatment of mice with morphine at different time points and in various behavioral assays.
source: For example, a module related to morphine response (module no. 2) consists of 17 different traits that were measured following treatment of mice with morphine at different time points and in various behavioral assays.
evidence: This describes the composition of module no. 2.

claim: Module no. 1 consists of two different traits measured following treatment with ethanol at different time points.
source: Similarly, a module related to an anxiety assay (module no. 1) consists of two different traits that were measured following treatment with ethanol at different time points.
evidence: This describes the composition of module no. 1.

claim: Module nos. 3, 4 and 5 suggest previously unknown connections between traits.
source: In contrast, and consistently with our goal of identifying novel relationships among traits, module nos. 3, 4 and 5 suggest previously unknown connections between traits.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of novel trait relationships.

claim: GEMOT's correlations among trait pairs were much stronger than expected by chance (p < 10^-200).
source: GEMOT's correlations among trait pairs were much stronger than expected by chance (p < 10−200), and were comparable to those obtained by the gene-based INVAMOD approach but weaker than those from the trait-based HC approach (p < 10−160; Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of GEMOT to other methods.

claim: GEMOT's trait pair correlations were comparable to those obtained by the gene-based INVAMOD approach.
source: GEMOT's correlations among trait pairs were much stronger than expected by chance (p < 10−200), and were comparable to those obtained by the gene-based INVAMOD approach but weaker than those from the trait-based HC approach (p < 10−160; Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This reports comparison of GEMOT to INVAMOD.

claim: GEMOT's trait pair correlations were weaker than those from the trait-based HC approach (p < 10^-160).
source: GEMOT's correlations among trait pairs were much stronger than expected by chance (p < 10−200), and were comparable to those obtained by the gene-based INVAMOD approach but weaker than those from the trait-based HC approach (p < 10−160; Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This reports comparison of GEMOT to HC approach.

claim: HC directly optimizes for trait-trait correlations.
source: This result was consistent with the fact that HC, but not GEMOT or INVAMOD, directly optimizes for such correlations.
evidence: This explains why HC has stronger trait correlations.

claim: GEMOT's predicted trait pairs were supported by the best-correlated transcripts across a wide range of trait-trait correlations.
source: We found that GEMOT's predicted trait pairs were supported by the best-correlated transcripts across a wide range of trait–trait correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,C).
evidence: This describes a property of GEMOT predictions with reference to figures.

claim: GEMOT outperforms the gene-based and random methods in transcript support (p < 10^-30 and p < 10^-50, respectively).
source: This analysis indicated that GEMOT outperforms the gene-based and random methods (p < 10−30 and p < 10−50, respectively) and is comparable to the trait-based method.
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of GEMOT to other methods.

claim: GEMOT is comparable to the trait-based method in transcript support.
source: This analysis indicated that GEMOT outperforms the gene-based and random methods (p < 10−30 and p < 10−50, respectively) and is comparable to the trait-based method.
evidence: This reports comparison of GEMOT to trait-based method.

claim: Module no. 2 consisted of 17 behavioral assays measuring responses to injection of morphine (50 mg/kg) over different periods of time.
source: The module consisted of a collection of 17 behavioral assays in the recombinant mouse strains, all carried out to measure their responses to injection of morphine (50 mg/kg, over different periods of time).
evidence: This describes the traits in module no. 2.

claim: Measured parameters in module no. 2 included distance traveled, place preference, and vertical activity.
source: Measured parameters included distance traveled, place preference, and vertical activity ([Philip et al., 2010]; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the specific measurements in module no. 2 with citation.

claim: All module no. 2 traits showed strong positive correlation with each other (|r| values ranged from 0.6 to 0.99).
source: All module traits showed a strong positive correlation with each other (|r| values ranged from 0.6 to 0.99, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and shared similar peaks within the genomic interval of module no. 2 (Figure 3A, top).
evidence: This reports the correlation values among traits in module no. 2 with reference to figures.

claim: Module no. 2 traits shared similar peaks within the genomic interval of module no. 2.
source: All module traits showed a strong positive correlation with each other (|r| values ranged from 0.6 to 0.99, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and shared similar peaks within the genomic interval of module no. 2 (Figure 3A, top).
evidence: This describes genetic association patterns in module no. 2 with reference to a figure.

claim: Module no. 2 consists of 32 driver transcripts including Klf7, p35, and Lrrk2.
source: Module no. 2 consists of a group of 32 driver transcripts (e.g., Klf7, p35, Lrrk2), all associated with the module's genotype and strongly correlated with each other and with the module traits (Figure 3A, bottom; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the driver transcripts in module no. 2 with reference to figures.

claim: All driver transcripts in module no. 2 are associated with the module's genotype and strongly correlated with each other and with the module traits.
source: Module no. 2 consists of a group of 32 driver transcripts (e.g., Klf7, p35, Lrrk2), all associated with the module's genotype and strongly correlated with each other and with the module traits (Figure 3A, bottom; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes properties of the driver transcripts with reference to figures.

claim: For all driver transcripts in module no. 2, causative relationships were much preferable to alternative relationships (p value ≤ 0.005, permutation-based FDR < 6 × 10^-5).
source: For all driver transcripts, the causative relationships were much preferable to the alternative relationships (p value ≤ 0.005, permutation-based FDR < 6 × 10−5, 'Materials and methods'; Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This reports statistical significance of causative relationships with reference to figures.

claim: Module no. 2 has two main groups of drivers.
source: We found two main groups of drivers (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the structure of drivers in module no. 2 with reference to figures.

claim: Group I consists of 21 genes whose transcript levels are negatively correlated with the morphine traits.
source: The first (denoted 'group I') consists of 21 genes whose transcript levels are negatively correlated with the morphine traits.
evidence: This describes group I in module no. 2.

claim: In group I, individuals carrying the DBA/2J allele have higher gene expression values than those carrying the C57BL/6J allele.
source: In this group, individuals carrying the DBA/2J allele in the module's variant have higher gene expression values than those of individuals carrying the C57BL/6J allele (e.g., Klf7 in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the genetic effect in group I with reference to a figure.

claim: Group II has the opposite correlation with the morphine traits and the opposite genetic effect compared to group I.
source: The second driver group (denoted 'group II') has the opposite correlation with the morphine traits and the opposite genetic effect (e.g., Idh1, in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes group II in module no. 2 with reference to a figure.

claim: For all module no. 2 traits, individuals carrying the C57BL/6J-allele have higher trait values.
source: These observations coincide with the fact that for all module traits, individuals carrying the C57BL/6J-allele have higher trait values (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This describes the genetic effect on traits with reference to figures.

claim: Causality p values in group I are more significant than in group II (p < 0.05, t-test).
source: Notably, causality p values in group I are more significant than in group II (p < 0.05, t-test; Figure 3C); one possible reason is that the two groups might relate to distinct mechanisms that differ in their causality strength.
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison between groups with a speculative explanation.

claim: Klf7 and Idh1 are the only two cis-associated module drivers in module no. 2.
source: Klf7 and Idh1 are the only two cis-associated module drivers and their causative role in mediating morphine traits is highly significant.
evidence: This identifies specific cis-associated drivers.

claim: The causative role of Klf7 and Idh1 in mediating morphine traits is highly significant.
source: Klf7 and Idh1 are the only two cis-associated module drivers and their causative role in mediating morphine traits is highly significant.
evidence: This describes the significance of Klf7 and Idh1.

claim: The causative p values of Klf7 on the remaining module transcripts were substantially more significant than the causative p values of Idh1 on those transcripts (p < 10^-7, K-S test).
source: Using these scores we found that the causative p values of Klf7 on the remaining module transcripts were substantially more significant than the causative p values of Idh1 on those transcripts (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, p < 10−7, K-S test).
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of Klf7 and Idh1 effects with reference to figures.

claim: Klf7, but not Idh1, likely affects the other module drivers, which in turn affect behavioral activity in response to morphine.
source: This finding holds for each of the driver groups I and II (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), suggesting that Klf7, but not Idh1, likely affects the other module drivers, which in turn affect behavioral activity in response to morphine.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the causality analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Klf7 is an activator of group I and a repressor of group II.
source: The finding of positive and negative correlations of Klf7 with the drivers in groups I and II is particularly intriguing because it suggests that Klf7 is an activator of group I and a repressor of group II (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation patterns with reference to a figure.

claim: Knockdown of Klf7 led to down-regulation of group I transcripts (p < 1.5 × 10^-5, FDR < 5 × 10^-5, t-test).
source: Indeed, whereas knockdown of Klf7 led to a down-regulation of group I transcripts (p < 1.5 × 10−5, FDR < 5 × 10−5, t-test), it had no influence in group II (p > 0.32; Figure 3G, left), in agreement with the predicted role of Klf7 as an activator and repressor of groups I and II, respectively.
evidence: This reports experimental validation results with reference to a figure.

claim: Knockdown of Klf7 had no influence on group II transcripts (p > 0.32).
source: Indeed, whereas knockdown of Klf7 led to a down-regulation of group I transcripts (p < 1.5 × 10−5, FDR < 5 × 10−5, t-test), it had no influence in group II (p > 0.32; Figure 3G, left), in agreement with the predicted role of Klf7 as an activator and repressor of groups I and II, respectively.
evidence: This reports experimental validation results with reference to a figure.

claim: The more significant the influence of Klf7 knockdown on a driver in group I, the stronger the causative role of the driver on behavioral morphine traits.
source: Furthermore, we found that the more significant the influence of Klf7 knockdown on a driver in group I, the stronger the causative role of the driver on behavioral morphine traits (Figure 3H).
evidence: This describes a relationship between experimental and computational results with reference to a figure.

claim: Overexpression of Klf7 led to significant down-regulation of transcripts in group II (p < 0.05, FDR < 0.06, t-test).
source: Overexpression of Klf7 had the opposite effect, with significant down-regulation of transcripts in group II (p < 0.05, FDR < 0.06, t-test) and even a small increase of transcripts in group I (p < 0.002, FDR < 0.005; Figure 3G, right), consistently with our model.
evidence: This reports experimental validation results with reference to a figure.

claim: Overexpression of Klf7 led to a small increase of transcripts in group I (p < 0.002, FDR < 0.005).
source: Overexpression of Klf7 had the opposite effect, with significant down-regulation of transcripts in group II (p < 0.05, FDR < 0.06, t-test) and even a small increase of transcripts in group I (p < 0.002, FDR < 0.005; Figure 3G, right), consistently with our model.
evidence: This reports experimental validation results with reference to a figure.

claim: Klf7 is a key driver mediating the effects of additional drivers in groups I and II, which in turn affect morphine response diversity.
source: Taken together, the two lines of evidence—both natural and experimental perturbations—indicated that Klf7 is a key driver mediating the effects of additional drivers in groups I and II, which in turn affect morphine response diversity (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence with reference to a figure.

claim: The p35 driver directly phosphorylates the opioid receptor.
source: For example, the p35/Cdk5 driver directly phosphorylates the opioid receptor (Xie et al., 2009; Pareek et al., 2012), and the morphine adduct MO-GSH is controlled by the Idh1 and Ggt1 drivers (Correia et al., 1984; Kumagai et al., 1990; Muller and Do, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism with citations.

claim: The morphine adduct MO-GSH is controlled by the Idh1 and Ggt1 drivers.
source: For example, the p35/Cdk5 driver directly phosphorylates the opioid receptor (Xie et al., 2009; Pareek et al., 2012), and the morphine adduct MO-GSH is controlled by the Idh1 and Ggt1 drivers (Correia et al., 1984; Kumagai et al., 1990; Muller and Do, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism with citations.

claim: The p35 driver affects cell migration through PAK inhibition.
source: Furthermore, morphine treatment may exert its action through cell migration and cell invasion processes (Gach et al., 2011): the p35 driver, as part of the p35/Cdk5 complex, affects the Rac/Cdc42 complex through PAK inhibition, resulting in altered cell migration (Nikolic et al., 1998), while the Mmp13 driver alters cell migration in response to morphine treatment because of its ability to degrade collagen (Gach et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a mechanism with citations.

claim: The Mmp13 driver alters cell migration in response to morphine treatment because of its ability to degrade collagen.
source: Furthermore, morphine treatment may exert its action through cell migration and cell invasion processes (Gach et al., 2011): the p35 driver, as part of the p35/Cdk5 complex, affects the Rac/Cdc42 complex through PAK inhibition, resulting in altered cell migration (Nikolic et al., 1998), while the Mmp13 driver alters cell migration in response to morphine treatment because of its ability to degrade collagen (Gach et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a mechanism with citations.

claim: Both Klf7 and Cdk5/p35 drivers activate p27 by expression or phosphorylation.
source: Both the Klf7 and the Cdk5/p35 drivers activate p27 by expression or phosphorylation (Laub et al., 2001; Smaldone et al., 2004), and p27 in turn affects the Rho GTPases Rac and RhoA, which then alter cell invasiveness and infiltration (Kawauchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes a mechanism with citations.

claim: p27 affects the Rho GTPases Rac and RhoA, which alter cell invasiveness and infiltration.
source: Both the Klf7 and the Cdk5/p35 drivers activate p27 by expression or phosphorylation (Laub et al., 2001; Smaldone et al., 2004), and p27 in turn affects the Rho GTPases Rac and RhoA, which then alter cell invasiveness and infiltration (Kawauchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes a mechanism with citations.

claim: In glioblastoma, the p27/Rho pathway affects infiltration of tumor cells.
source: In glioblastoma, for example, the p27/Rho pathway affects infiltration of tumor cells (Ruiz-Ontañon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism with citation.

claim: All four top-ranked Klf7-mediated drivers attain significant effects on survival of patients with glioblastoma (Kaplan-Meier p < 1 × 10^-11, 1.4 × 10^-4, 1 × 10^-4 and 0.01 for Ntng2, p35, Rexo2 and Lrrk2, respectively; FDR < 0.05).
source: In agreement with this prediction, using the Rembrandt database (Madhavan et al., 2009) we found that all four top-ranked Klf7-mediated drivers attain significant effects on survival of patients with glioblastoma (Kaplan–Meier p < 1 × 10−11, 1.4 × 10−4, 1 × 10−4 and 0.01 for the four drivers Ntng2, p35, Rexo2 and Lrrk2, respectively; in all cases, FDR < 0.05, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), supporting the role of module no. 2 in cell invasiveness.
evidence: This reports analysis of human data supporting the model with reference to a figure.

claim: The Klf7 transcript is up-regulated in response to morphine (being one of the top ten up-regulated genes).
source: For example, the Klf7 transcript is up-regulated in response to morphine (being one of the top ten up-regulated genes [Suzuki et al., 2003]).
evidence: This is stated as a known finding with citation.

claim: Both the p35 driver and its activated protein Cdk5 were up-regulated in response to acute morphine but down-regulated on exposure to chronic morphine.
source: Both the p35 driver and its activated protein Cdk5 were up-regulated in response to acute morphine but down-regulated on exposure to chronic morphine (Ferrer-Alcón et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a known finding with citation.

claim: Idh1 and Ggt1 drivers are responsible for the synthesis and degradation, respectively, of the reduced form of glutathione (GSH).
source: The coregulated Idh1 and Ggt1 drivers (Muller and Do, 2012) are responsible for the synthesis and degradation, respectively, of the reduced form of glutathione (GSH).
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism with citation.

claim: A conjugated form of morphine and GSH (MO-GSH) attains higher morphine reactivity.
source: A conjugated form of morphine and GSH (MO-GSH) attains higher morphine reactivity (Correia et al., 1984; Kumagai et al., 1990) that may alter the morphine responses.
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism with citations.

claim: Key roles of Klf7 have been reported primarily in neurons.
source: However, whereas key roles of Klf7 have been reported primarily in neurons (Bieker, 2001; Laub et al., 2005), here we found a causative effect of Klf7 on behavioral responses to morphine that was specific to myeloid tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This contrasts previous knowledge with the current finding, with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: A causative effect of Klf7 on behavioral responses to morphine was specific to myeloid tissue.
source: However, whereas key roles of Klf7 have been reported primarily in neurons (Bieker, 2001; Laub et al., 2005), here we found a causative effect of Klf7 on behavioral responses to morphine that was specific to myeloid tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study with reference to a figure.

claim: Morphine injection leads to a reduction in neutrophil infiltration 30-120 min after treatment.
source: Furthermore, morphine injection leads to a reduction in neutrophil infiltration 30–120 min after treatment (Clark et al., 2007), in agreement with the timing of causative relationships between Klf7 and behavioral assays at 30–120 min after morphine injection (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated as a known finding with citation, and connected to the current results.

claim: In vivo behavioral responses to morphine are affected not only by neuronal activity, but also through certain components of the immune system.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that in vivo behavioral responses to morphine are affected not only by neuronal activity, but also through certain components of the immune system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: Module no. 3 consists of a genomic interval in chr4:133-142 Mbp and five correlated traits: pain response (thermal nociception), lens weight, eye weight (with or without correction for brain weight), and ethanol response (place preference).
source: Module no. 3 (Figure 4A) shows the ability of GEMOT to group a variety of distinct traits. This module consists of a genomic interval in chr4:133–142 Mbp and five correlated traits, namely pain response (thermal nociception [Philip et al., 2010]), lens weight (Zhou and Williams, 1999), eye weight (with or without correction for brain weight [Zhou and Williams, 1999]), and ethanol response (place preference [Cunningham, 1995]).
evidence: This describes the composition of module no. 3 with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: All traits in module no. 3 were strongly intercorrelated, with |r| values ranging from 0.67 to 0.9.
source: All traits were found to be strongly intercorrelated, with |r| values ranging from 0.67 to 0.9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This reports correlation values with reference to a figure.

claim: Eya3 and Cd52 were proposed as cis-associated drivers in module no. 3.
source: Eya3 and Cd52 were proposed as cis-associated drivers, a suggestion further supported by the known role of Eya3 in eye development (Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013) and the involvement of Cd52 in pain signaling (Poh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a prediction from GEMOT supported by citations.

claim: Eya3 has a known role in eye development.
source: Eya3 and Cd52 were proposed as cis-associated drivers, a suggestion further supported by the known role of Eya3 in eye development (Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013) and the involvement of Cd52 in pain signaling (Poh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as known information with citation.

claim: Cd52 is involved in pain signaling.
source: Eya3 and Cd52 were proposed as cis-associated drivers, a suggestion further supported by the known role of Eya3 in eye development (Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013) and the involvement of Cd52 in pain signaling (Poh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as known information with citation.

claim: The significant causative role of Eya3 and Cd52 can be found along the entire myeloid pathway but not in lymphoid, eye, or brain tissues.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows that the significant causative role of these drivers can be found along the entire myeloid pathway (including stem cells [Lin−Sca-1+c-Kit+], common progenitors of the myeloid and erythroid lineages [Lin−Sca-1−c-Kit+], erythroid [TER-119+] and myeloid [Gr-1+] lineages), but not when using data from the lymphoid, eye, or brain tissues.
evidence: This describes tissue specificity analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Eya3 and Cd52 play a role in pain processes and eye conditions mainly through their functionality in myeloid cells.
source: This suggests that Eya3 and Cd52 play a role in pain processes and eye conditions mainly through their functionality in myeloid cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tissue specificity analysis.

claim: Module no. 4 consists of a genomic interval in chr11:8-19 Mbp and five traits: measures of two hippocampal structures, locomotor response to cocaine, number of liver tumors, and number of haematopoietic stem cells.
source: Module no. 4 (Figure 4B) demonstrates GEMOT's ability to identify a group of traits that show weak correlations among themselves, but share the same driver transcripts. The module consists of a genomic interval in chr11:8–19 Mbp and five traits: the measures of two hippocampal structures (volume and age-related lesions) from two distinct publications (Jucker et al., 2000; Martin et al., 2006), locomotor response to cocaine (Philip et al., 2010), number of liver tumors (Lee et al., 1995), and number of haematopoietic stem cells (Liang et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the composition of module no. 4 with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Module no. 4 traits show weak and moderate correlations, with |r| values ranging from 0.01 to 0.58.
source: The module's traits show weak and moderate correlations, with |r| values ranging from 0.01 to 0.58 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This reports correlation values with reference to a figure.

claim: Ythdf2 and Aldh6a1 were predicted as the top drivers in module no. 4.
source: Of six suggested drivers, Ythdf2 and Aldh6a1 were predicted as the top drivers (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: This is a prediction from GEMOT with reference to a figure.

claim: Aldh6a1 is involved in brain structure.
source: The validity of this prediction is supported by the known involvement of Aldh6a1 in brain structure (Marcadier et al., 2013), and is further supported by a recent report (Meyer and Jaffrey, 2014) that N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNA, whose readers are Ythdf1–3, causes an altered locomotor response to cocaine.
evidence: This is stated as known information with citation.

claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNA, whose readers are Ythdf1-3, causes an altered locomotor response to cocaine.
source: The validity of this prediction is supported by the known involvement of Aldh6a1 in brain structure (Marcadier et al., 2013), and is further supported by a recent report (Meyer and Jaffrey, 2014) that N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of RNA, whose readers are Ythdf1–3, causes an altered locomotor response to cocaine.
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with citation.

claim: In module no. 4, a significant causative role was found in myeloid cells, but not in brain, eye, liver, or lymphoid tissue.
source: In this module, a significant causative role was found in myeloid cells, but not in brain, eye, liver, or lymphoid tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting a novel function of myeloid cells in regulating neurobiological and behavioral traits—an intriguing possibility that warrants future investigation.
evidence: This describes tissue specificity with reference to a figure and suggests a novel finding.

claim: GEMOT displayed the best accuracy for noise levels ranging between 0.25 and 1, with lower accuracy for higher noise levels.
source: GEMOT displayed the best accuracy for noise levels ranging between 0.25 and 1, with lower accuracy for higher noise levels.
evidence: This reports performance evaluation results.

claim: Sub-networks with a noise level that do not exceed 1 are more likely to represent real biological modules.
source: Analysis of various network properties in both mouse and synthetic data shows that sub-networks with a noise level that do not exceed 1 are more likely to represent real biological modules (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: GEMOT's accuracy remained high with an increasing number of traits.
source: Unlike the compared methods, GEMOT's accuracy remained high with an increasing number of traits (Figure 5C); similar results were obtained for alternative network structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This reports performance comparison with reference to figures.

claim: In simulation, GEMOT outperformed the compared algorithms in handling a growing number of traits and in identifying the correct groups of traits when using biologically-relevant parameters.
source: Overall, in our simulation, GEMOT outperformed the compared algorithms in handling a growing number of traits and in identifying the correct groups of traits when using biologically-relevant parameters.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the simulation study.

claim: GEMOT attains higher accuracy than compared methods in discerning traits that share the same driver transcripts.
source: The analysis suggested that although all compared methods successfully discern all traits in a sub-network (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A), GEMOT attains higher accuracy in discerning those traits that share the same driver transcripts (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This reports comparison results with reference to figures.

claim: GEMOT succeeded in discriminating the correct subsets of co-regulated traits because it is tailored for identification of causative relationships.
source: Notably, the GEMOT algorithm is tailored for identification of causative relationships, unlike the compared methods, explaining why GEMOT succeeded in discriminating the correct subsets of co-regulated traits.
evidence: This explains why GEMOT performs better than other methods.

claim: GEMOT results highlighted three types of high-order organization of traits: groups of tightly related traits sharing the same transcripts mechanisms, groups of distinct traits sharing the same transcripts mechanism but not necessarily high correlations, and different groups commonly having overlapping traits but differing in their underlying mechanisms.
source: Our results in mice highlighted three types of high-order organization of traits. (i) Groups of tightly related traits that share the same transcripts mechanisms (modules 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, e.g., Figure 3). (ii) Groups of distinct traits that share the same transcripts mechanism, but not necessarily high correlations among them (modules 3, 4, 5, e.g., Figure 4). (iii) Different groups commonly have overlapping traits, but typically differ in their underlying mechanisms (Figure 2B).
evidence: This summarizes the main findings with references to figures.

claim: GEMOT is superior to previous trait-grouping methods in directly filtering and validating causative transcripts.
source: Whereas previous trait-grouping methods have used genetic or molecular data separately, and thus did not validate causative transcripts (e.g., Shi et al., 2010; Gat-Viks et al., 2013; as illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), the GEMOT method aims at directly filtering and validating such relationships.
evidence: This compares GEMOT to previous methods with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: GEMOT is superior to previous trait-grouping methods in identifying trait groups that share the same underlying transcripts.
source: Our simulations showed that GEMOT is superior to these methods in identifying trait groups that share the same underlying transcripts (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This reports simulation results with reference to a figure.

claim: Network reconstruction methods are limited in their scalability and may be particularly inefficient when applied on a large number of components.
source: Whereas these methods are limited in their scalability and may be particularly inefficient when applied on a large number of components, our approach can be scaled to larger networks, but can construct the network only partially.
evidence: This compares GEMOT to network reconstruction methods.

claim: GEMOT can be scaled to larger networks, but can construct the network only partially.
source: Whereas these methods are limited in their scalability and may be particularly inefficient when applied on a large number of components, our approach can be scaled to larger networks, but can construct the network only partially.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of GEMOT.

claim: GEMOT is more scalable than alternative network construction methods in terms of both running time and accuracy under increased network sizes.
source: For example, in comparing both running time and accuracy under increased network sizes we found GEMOT to be more scalable than the alternative network construction methods (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplements 2B, 4B).
evidence: This reports comparison results with reference to figures.

claim: GEMOT can be applied on a compendium of molecular data from multiple tissues to simultaneously identify both the biological mechanism and its relevant tissue.
source: One possibility is that GEMOT will be applied on a compendium of molecular data from multiple tissues. In such cases, GEMOT predictions can be used to simultaneously identify both the biological mechanism and its relevant tissue.
evidence: This describes a potential future application of GEMOT.

claim: GEMOT is applicable to a variety of molecular data types in addition to gene-expression data.
source: Second, GEMOT is applicable to a variety of molecular data types in addition to gene-expression data.
evidence: This describes the generalizability of GEMOT.

claim: Application of GEMOT to blood cytokines or plasma lipids is expected to identify molecular factors acting at the cell-cell communication level.
source: For example, its application in blood cytokines or plasma lipids (Teslovich et al., 2010) is expected to make it possible to identify molecular factors acting at the cell–cell communication level.
evidence: This describes a potential application with citation.

claim: Future extensions of GEMOT may provide means to include environmental factors as part of the module.
source: Similarly, future extensions of GEMOT may provide the means to include environmental factors as part of the module.
evidence: This describes a potential future extension.

claim: Monitoring of additional strains would allow discriminating between several alternative genomic intervals for the same module.
source: Third, monitoring of additional strains would allow discriminating between several alternative genomic intervals for the same module, which may arise due to linkage disequilibrium between chromosomally distinct loci.
evidence: This describes a potential improvement to the method.

claim: Characterization of GEMOT modules that share a similar collection of traits but have different genomic intervals may reflect gene-gene interactions that lead to connections among traits.
source: Fourth, characterization of GEMOT modules that share a similar collection of traits but have different genomic intervals may reflect gene–gene interactions that lead to connections among traits.
evidence: This describes a potential application for understanding gene interactions.

claim: GEMOT can potentially be further improved by the construction of internal causative relationships within the transcripts and the traits layers.
source: Finally, GEMOT can potentially be further improved by the construction of internal causative relationships within the transcripts and the traits layers.
evidence: This describes a potential future improvement.

claim: GEMOT cannot distinguish cases of multiple drivers that are part of the same regulatory circuit from cases of multiple drivers that act through several distinct circuits.
source: It should be noted, however, that GEMOT cannot distinguish cases of multiple drivers that are part of the same regulatory circuit from cases of multiple drivers that act through several distinct circuits.
evidence: This describes a limitation of GEMOT.

claim: GEMOT predictions provide biological or clinical hypotheses for additional experimental investigations.
source: Rather, its predictions provide biological or clinical hypotheses for additional experimental investigations.
evidence: This describes the intended use of GEMOT results.

claim: GEMOT methodology is general and can be applied to the study of other taxa.
source: Because the GEMOT methodology is a general one and can be applied to the study of other taxa, this approach may facilitate our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying human disease.
evidence: This describes the generalizability and potential impact of GEMOT.
